syllabus.clause: 2¹⁶-value chunks stored as array, bitmap or run containers chosen per chunk
used for bitmap indexes and posting lists in Lucene, Druid, Pinot and Spark

sources.source: Chambi, Lemire, Kaser and Godin, "Better Bitmap Performance with Roaring Bitmaps"

items.item: The two-level structure: 65,536 chunks by top 16 bits, each a sorted (key, container) pair, container holding the low 16 bits
Array container ≤4,096 values at 2 bytes each; bitmap container above that, a fixed 8,192 bytes
Array-array intersection: a simple merge when cardinalities are within 64x of each other, galloping once one dwarfs the other
"2x smaller" and "up to 900x faster for intersections," each the paper's own benchmark

sources.source: Lemire, Ssi-Yan-Kai and Kaser, "Consistently Faster and Smaller Compressed Bitmaps with Roaring"

items.item: Run container: 2 + 4r bytes for r runs; runOptimize scans existing containers and converts to run containers only when smaller, typically once before storing
"Up to two orders of magnitude" faster, and the Lucene/Spark/Kylin/Druid adoption sentence
The two serialization cookies (12346, 12347) and the run-container serialized layout
Two separate Roaring-inspired classes, each with its own 65,536-value-block, 4,096-threshold shape, read directly from their javadoc rather than from the Roaring papers' own adoption claim

expert.by: self-review (no independent reviewer this session; see REVIEW.md)

items.item: Why a chunk's own container is picked by measuring, not by a fixed rule tied to count alone — the same hundred values scattered versus bunched can favor different containers

at.step: Does the same container win both?

items.item: Why the 4,096 threshold falls straight out of two bytes per value against a fixed eight kilobytes, never a tuned constant
Why a run container's cost tracks run count, almost never value count — a single run spanning a whole 65,536-value chunk still costs six bytes
Why a chunk key missing from one side of an intersection costs nothing at all — the two sorted key lists are merged like any two sorted lists, never computed and discarded

at.step: What does a missing chunk cost?

items.item: Why galloping wins decisively only once one side of an intersection dwarfs the other, and costs no more than a plain merge when the two are close in size
That the two Lucene classes are Roaring-inspired, independently-varied code, not the RoaringBitmap library itself — stated explicitly rather than left for the reader to assume

Why the array/bitmap crossover formula generalizes beyond the specific 65,536-value chunk size: the same two cost formulas set equal to each other would give a different crossover count for a differently sized chunk, so the number itself is a consequence of the chunk size chosen, not a fact about containers in general

Why picking a container per chunk can never do worse than committing to one container for the whole set: the worst case for the per-chunk approach is that every chunk happens to prefer the same container, which is exactly the plain-structure case
That the chapter's own dense/sparse/clustered predicates are shape stand-ins for the hook's literal log predicates, not real log semantics

That Roaring is the chapter's exact counterpart to Bloom's approximate one — no false answers, in close to the honest minimum each chunk's own shape allows — and that this exactness is itself still compressible further, which is where integer compression picks up
